differentiation.extension: Choose one event (Estates-General split, Tennis Court Oath, or Bastille). Using only the evidence you collected, write a 3-sentence argument that explains how your side's causes made that event more likely, and add one sentence that uses a competing interpretation from the other side to show cause and context together.
differentiation.support: If you cannot start, use this sentence frame and one worked example. Frame: 'I think X was central because the chapter says "_____" (quote) which shows _____. Another example is "_____" which shows _____.' Worked example (for political/financial side): 'I think political and financial crises were central because the chapter says "the crown faced bankruptcy and indecisive policy" which shows the monarchy could not manage the crisis. Another example is "tax reforms failed and ministers resigned" which shows resistance to reform made the situation worse.' Partner with a stronger reader if needed.

materials: One textbook or chapter copy per student
One printed slip per pair with their assigned position and two evidence prompts (teacher prepares in 5 minutes)
Timer or stopwatch
Whiteboard or chart paper and marker
student_instructions: You are in a pair. Your teacher gave your pair a slip that assigns which side you argue: either 'Political/financial crisis' OR 'Social/economic pressures'.

Step 1 (4 minutes): Use your textbook chapter to find two short pieces of evidence (one sentence each) that support your assigned side. Write each sentence on the slip under 'Text evidence 1' and 'Text evidence 2'.

Step 2 (debate): Partner A speaks for 1 minute using both pieces of evidence to make a claim about why their factor was central. Partner B then speaks for 1 minute using their evidence to disagree and offer an alternative cause. After both speak, you have 1 minute to prepare a 30-second joint conclusion that names at least one piece of evidence the other side raised and one reason both factors mattered together.

When finished, be ready to share your joint conclusion aloud if called on. Finally, write one sentence connecting your evidence to either the Estates-General/Third Estate actions, the Tennis Court Oath, or the storming of the Bastille.
success_criteria: Each pair has two written textbook sentences on their slip labeled 'Text evidence 1' and 'Text evidence 2'.
During speaking time each partner gives a clear claim supported by at least one textbook sentence from their slip.
Joint conclusions named one piece of the other side's evidence and stated how two types of causes can combine (observed for chosen pairs or on the board list).
teacher_instructions: 1. Arrange students in pairs. Tell pairs they will hold a two-minute debate where one partner argues that political and financial crises were the main cause of 1789, and the other argues that social and economic pressures were the main cause. Hand each pair a printed slip with their positions and two lines labelled 'Text evidence 1' and 'Text evidence 2'.

2. Give pairs 4 minutes to find two pieces of evidence in their textbook chapter (one sentence each) that support their assigned position. Circulate and quietly point to likely paragraph headings if a pair is stuck; do not give the answers. After 4 minutes announce time.

3. Start the debate rounds: partner A speaks for 1 minute presenting their evidence and claim; partner B speaks for 1 minute responding with their evidence and a short counterpoint. After both have spoken, allow 1 minute for both to prepare a 30-second joint conclusion that acknowledges at least one competing interpretation. Run the timer and signal when to switch.

4. After pairs finish, ask two pairs (choose volunteers or nominate) to read their joint conclusion aloud (30 seconds each). As they speak, record on the board one piece of evidence each pair used and one competing interpretation they acknowledged.

5. Conclude by reminding students the Tennis Court Oath, the Third Estate's break in May 1789, and the Bastille's symbolic fall on 14 July 1789; ask students to copy one line under their notes that connects their debate evidence to these events (30 seconds).
activities.title: Mini Debate: What Sparked the Revolution?

differentiation.extension: Choose one event on the class timeline and write a two-sentence alternative interpretation that challenges the simple cause-effect story. For example: argue that the Declaration of the Rights of Man reflected ongoing political conflict rather than full agreement — name one line of evidence from other events (like the August Decrees or the Flight to Varennes) that supports your alternative interpretation.
differentiation.support: Pair students heterogeneously so a stronger reader pairs with a weaker reader. Provide this sentence frame to use when writing the one-sentence explanation: “The Third Estate (or National Assembly) [action verb] by _______________, which shows they were trying to _______________ (link to one concept). Evidence: ‘___________’ (underlined excerpt).” As a worked example, show a filled box: “The National Assembly declared itself the law-making body (action) to end the old order (purpose). Evidence: ‘The representatives of the Third Estate... constituted themselves a National Assembly.’”

materials: Copies of short primary excerpts (printed slips) — one excerpt per pair: Tennis Court Oath (abridged), August Decrees summary, Declaration of the Rights of Man excerpt, short account of the Flight to Varennes (all provided by the teacher)
Blank timeline strip per group (one sheet of paper long enough for 6 boxes) or 6 sticky notes per group
Pens or pencils
Stopwatch or visible clock
student_instructions: 1. In your pair, read the excerpt on your slip silently. Underline one sentence that shows a concrete action linked to the Revolution (for example: forming a new assembly, voting to abolish feudal dues, issuing a declaration, or arresting the king).

2. Decide together: what action does that sentence show the Third Estate (or the National Assembly) taking? Write a one-sentence explanation that names the action and links it to one of these concepts: August Decrees, Declaration of the Rights of Man, Constitutional Monarchy phase, or Flight to Varennes.

3. Put your one-sentence explanation on one box of the timeline strip or on one sticky note. Place it where you think it belongs in sequence from May 1789 (Estates-General called) to September 1792 (end of constitutional monarchy).
4. After placing it, be ready to point to the underlined sentence in the excerpt as the evidence for your placement when the teacher comes by or when a neighboring pair checks your work.
success_criteria: Each pair has an underlined sentence on their excerpt that they can point to as evidence for the action they named.
Each timeline box/sticky shows a one-sentence explanation that links the action to one of the four required concepts and is placed in a plausible sequence.
At least one pair can explain aloud how their cited sentence supports their placement when asked (reads the sentence and states the connection).
teacher_instructions: 1. Arrange students in pairs. Hand each pair one printed excerpt slip and one blank timeline strip or set of 6 sticky notes. Say: “You have 12 minutes. Use the excerpt you were given to identify the key action by the Third Estate and place it in the correct order on the timeline strip. Then prepare a one-sentence explanation that links that action to at least one of the four concepts listed on the wall: August Decrees, Declaration of the Rights of Man, Constitutional Monarchy period, or Flight to Varennes.”

2. Tell pairs to spend the first 5 minutes reading their excerpt silently and underlining one sentence that shows an action taken by the Third Estate. If the excerpt does not name the Third Estate explicitly, they should note who acted (e.g., National Assembly) and why that counts as the Third Estate acting. Start the timer.

3. After 5 minutes, ask pairs to use the next 4 minutes to decide where their action fits in sequence (relative to calling of the Estates-General, Tennis Court Oath, creation of National Constituent Assembly, August Decrees, Declaration, Constitutional Monarchy, Flight to Varennes). They write a one-sentence explanation on their timeline box/sticky note and place it in order. Circulate; check that each pair points to the sentence they underlined as evidence for their chosen action.

4. In the final 3 minutes, ask pairs to swap their timeline quickly with a neighboring pair for a 30-second quick check: the neighbor reads the sentence and either nods or raises a hand if they think the placement is wrong. Return timelines. End by asking one or two pairs to read their one-sentence explanation aloud. Collect timelines or leave them displayed.

5. While students work, listen for pairs explicitly citing the excerpt sentence as evidence, and prompt any pair that treats events as single-cause stories to consider another interpretation (for example: did the Declaration reflect consensus or were there further disputes?).
activities.title: Tracing Actions: Third Estate from Estates-General to Constitutional Monarchy

differentiation.extension: Challenge question for early finishers: Prepare a 90–120 second mini-argument (in role) that compares two competing interpretations of assignats: one that says they solved the fiscal crisis by using confiscated church property, and one that says they caused long-term economic problems. Cite at least two items from the factsheet as evidence and propose one additional primary-source question you would ask to decide between these interpretations.
differentiation.support: If you are unsure how to start, use this sentence frame: “As a [role], I support/oppose [measure from factsheet] because [brief factual reason from factsheet].” Example worked first statement for a Moderate deputy: “As a moderate deputy, I accept the proclamation of the Republic on 22 September 1792 (Year I) but worry that the Law of Suspects leads to too many arrests without fair trials.” Pair a struggling student with a stronger reader in the same group if needed.

materials: Printed role slip per student (4 roles per group) — teacher prepares 1 set per group in 10 minutes

One copy per group of a short factsheet (one-sided) summarising: proclamation of the Republic (22 Sep 1792, Year I), assignats (backed by confiscated church property), Law of Suspects, Law of 22 Prairial, drownings at Nantes, executions of Hébertists, Danton, and Robespierre, dates for the Reign of Terror (Sept 1793–2 July 1794)
Timer or stopwatch (phone)
Small paper and pen per student
Optional: classroom whiteboard or chart paper for quick group notes
student_instructions: You are a delegate in the National Convention in late 1793. Read your role slip and the factsheet.
You have 2 minutes to prepare one 60–90 second statement in role. Use only the factsheet for facts and the role’s viewpoint to choose which facts to stress.

When it is your turn (each group has 6 minutes total), speak in character for 60–90 seconds. Say one clear claim (e.g., ‘We must keep the Law of Suspects’) and cite at least one specific item from the factsheet (date, law name, or event).

After all four in your group speak, work together for 3 minutes to write one sentence that summarises, using the factsheet, the Convention’s main measures and the human costs of the Terror that you can all agree on.
Be ready to read your group’s one-sentence resolution aloud.
success_criteria: Each student speaker cites at least one specific item from the factsheet (for example: ‘Law of Suspects’, ‘assignats backed by confiscated church property’, ‘22 September 1792, Year I’, or named events like ‘drownings at Nantes’).

Each group produces a one-sentence resolution that mentions at least one measure (assignats, emergency laws, or proclamation of the Republic) and at least one human cost (mass arrests/executions, named executions, or Law of 22 Prairial).
At least two different groups present competing interpretations (for example: one group defends assignats as necessary while another highlights negative consequences).
teacher_instructions: 1. Arrange students into groups of four. Give each student one role slip and each group one factsheet. Say: “You are delegates in the National Convention in late 1793. Your job is to prepare a 60–90 second statement from your role’s perspective about the Republic’s recent measures (assignats, emergency laws) and the human costs of the Terror.” Start the timer for 2 minutes of preparation.

2. While groups prepare, circulate to check they use only evidence on the factsheet and to prompt with two questions if stuck: “Which measure on the factsheet supports your view?” and “Name one human cost from the factsheet you want to highlight.” Do not give new facts.

3. After 2 minutes, call groups to perform. Each group has 6 minutes total: each of the four students speaks for 60–90 seconds in role (teacher times with stopwatch). Announce: “Begin the Convention statements now.” While groups perform, take quick notes of which facts each student cites.

4. After all groups present (or after 6 minutes of presentations if rotating groups), give each group 3 minutes to prepare a one-sentence group resolution that summarises the main measures and human costs they agree on using only items from the factsheet. Then ask one group volunteer to read the resolution aloud.

5. Close by reading aloud (or pointing to) one competing interpretation: e.g., “Some delegates argue assignats were necessary to stabilise finance; others say they created inflation and did not solve the crisis.” Ask students to listen for which side used which piece of evidence during presentations.
activities.title: Convention Debate: Republic, Assignats, and the Terror

differentiation.extension: Choose one piece of evidence you found that could support more than one interpretation. Write a 6–8 sentence paragraph (to be handed in) that explains which interpretation that evidence supports best, and then present an alternative interpretation using a different piece of evidence from the charts. Cite both locations in the chapter.
differentiation.support: Pair lower-readiness students with a stronger reader. Give that pair a worked example card: 'Worked example (station A): "The chapter records Robespierre invoking 'natural rights' in his speech (p. 18, para. 2) — evidence for Enlightenment influence."' Also provide a reduced task: at two stations (A and C) they only need to find one highlighted sentence in the chapter and copy it with the citation.

materials: Class set of the chapter (one per student) or projected excerpts
4 sheets of chart paper taped to walls or desks
Markers (at least one per pair)
Printed slip per pair with two prompts (see teacher) — can be photocopied in 5 minutes
Timer or stopwatch
student_instructions: 1. Work with your partner. You will visit four stations for 2 minutes each. At each station read the heading and the short prompt on the slip.

2. Use the chapter in front of you (or the projected excerpt) to find one specific piece of evidence that supports the station heading. Evidence can be a quoted phrase, a named event or a figure (e.g., numbers of soldiers, dates), and you must write the page or paragraph number after your sentence.

3. On the chart paper write one clear sentence: say which interpretation or fact the evidence supports and give the citation. Example: 'The chapter quotes a deputy saying “rights” were the goal (p. 42, para. 3) — supports Enlightenment-driven view.'
4. After 2 minutes, rotate to the next station clockwise until you have visited all four. At the last station add one short question about conflicting evidence for classmates to answer later.
success_criteria: At each station most chart entries name a specific piece of evidence from the chapter and include a page or paragraph citation.
Pairs can be heard briefly explaining to the teacher which line or figure in the chapter supports the sentence they write.
The 'Wartime mobilization' station contains at least two entries that cite chapter figures (e.g., numbers of troops, years, or territorial gains) rather than only general statements.
teacher_instructions: 1. Before class tape four chart papers around the room and write one heading on each: A) 'Enlightenment-driven view', B) 'Pragmatic/Immediate Causes view', C) 'Wartime mobilization: scale & figures (1792–1795)', D) 'Questions & competing evidence'. Place one printed prompt slip at each paper for the first pair; give each pair one slip when they start.

2. Tell students: 'You will do a 10-minute gallery walk in pairs. At each station you will read the prompt, find one piece of evidence in the chapter that supports the heading, and write a short sentence on the chart naming the evidence and which page/paragraph it came from. Rotate every 2 minutes so each pair visits all four stations.' Assign students into pairs and hand each pair a copy of the printed prompt slip and a marker.

3. Start the timer for 2-minute rotations. At each rotation announce verbally 'Rotate' and cue pairs to move clockwise. While students move, circulate quickly: listen for one sentence from a pair at a station, check that they cite a specific line or figure from the chapter, and remind them to write the page/paragraph number with their sentence.

4. After the four rotations (8 minutes of stations plus 2 minutes for transitions = 10 minutes), ask pairs to return to seats. Spend the final minute asking two pairs to read aloud one evidence sentence they wrote for station A and one for station C. Collect chart papers or leave them visible for later reference.
activities.title: Gallery Walk: Two Interpretations and Wartime Change

differentiation.extension: For early finishers: write a two-sentence mini-argument (on the back of your slip) comparing two competing interpretations from the chapter: (a) the Convention’s abolition of slavery in 1794 as principled vs (b) as a pragmatic response to colonial uprisings — include one chapter quote supporting each interpretation and state which you find more convincing and why.
differentiation.support: Pair a student who finished the chapter with one who skimmed it. Give the struggling student this sentence frame to complete at each stop: 'The chapter says __________, so this shows __________.' Example (worked first item for Prompt A): 'The chapter says the Jacobin Club was closed after Robespierre fell, so this shows a political reaction aimed at removing Jacobin power.'

materials: one printed slip per pair with four short prompts (teacher prepares in 5–10 minutes)
clipboards or hard surface for writing (or textbook as lap board)
two pens or pencils per pair
stopwatch or phone timer (teacher only)
class list or seating chart to record pair numbers
student_instructions: You are in a pair. Each pair has one printed slip with four prompts labeled A, B, C, D and a clipboard and two pens.

We will walk to four short stops in order: A, B, C, D. At each stop read only the prompt matching that label on your slip and write one clear sentence that answers it using evidence from the chapter you read.
Prompts (examples you will see):
- A (Thermidor): Cite one action taken after Robespierre’s fall and one piece of chapter evidence showing it was revenge or negotiation.
- B (Slavery & colonies): Give one change in policy toward Saint-Domingue between 1791–1793 and the chapter line that explains its effect.
- C (Media & symbols / Women): Name one way newspapers or symbols were used, or one way women were politically active, and quote the chapter phrase that supports it.
- D (Economy / Assignats): State one immediate legal/economic change (e.g., tithes, church land, assignats) and one practical difficulty the chapter reports when implementing it.
Spend 2.5 minutes at each stop. Write one sentence only—include the exact phrase or short citation from the chapter if you can. If you are unsure how to start, use the sentence frame on your slip.
When the teacher calls time, stop writing and return to your seat with your slip face down on the clipboard.
success_criteria: Most pairs stop at each labeled station and write one sentence that includes a specific phrase or short citation from the chapter (observable on slips).
At least half the pairs cite an explicit chapter detail that distinguishes the Thermidorian revenge actions from negotiated treaties (e.g., executions in the south versus negotiated peace).

Several slips correctly name a practical difficulty implementing the August Decrees or using assignats (e.g., enforcement problems, inflation) rather than making a general claim that the decrees simply worked.
teacher_instructions: 1. Before class, cut the printed slips so each pair receives one. Each slip lists four labeled prompts (A–D) tied to the concepts below. Arrange students in pairs by handing them sequential pair numbers as they enter.

2. Explain the task aloud: 'You will do a 10-minute field walk around the classroom and adjacent corridor. At four stations you will stop, read a prompt, and write a one-sentence answer grounded in the chapter evidence. I will call time and rotate you. Focus on the specific evidence named in each prompt — not on outside facts.' Start the timer for 10 minutes then say 'Go.'

3. While pairs circulate, call out the station rotations every 2.5 minutes so pairs stop at each of the four labeled locations: A (near the door), B (by the windows), C (by the whiteboard), D (in the corridor). At each stop pairs read only the prompt on their slip for that label and write one sentence responding with evidence from the chapter. Circulate and read students' answers silently, correcting obvious factual errors by quietly showing the relevant line number on the printed slip if they misread the prompt.

4. With 1 minute left, call 'final sentence' so pairs finish and tuck slips under their clipboards. Collect slips as students return to seats. Use remaining minute to say: 'Which two common mistakes about the Bastille and assignats should we watch for in discussion?' and write two student answers on the board.
5. End by quickly sorting collected slips into two piles: answers that cite specific chapter evidence and answers that make unsupported claims. Keep these for the next class discussion.
activities.title: Revolutionary Aftershocks Walk-and-Record

differentiation.extension: Prepare a 3-minute mini-response: analyze how the symbol of the guillotine (use Opie 1997 slip) complicates a simple positive or negative judgement about long-term impact. Does its symbolic power strengthen the argument that the Revolution created modern political norms, or does it show limits to that claim? Cite at least one other bibliography entry from the slips to support your nuanced answer.
differentiation.support: If students cannot start: pair them with a stronger partner (teacher-assigned). Provide this sentence frame to begin an opening: 'I argue that the Revolution did/did not create a modern nation-state because [brief reason]. Evidence A/B supports this by saying [quote three to eight words].' Also give a worked example: Pro opening sentence: 'I argue the Revolution created modern nation-states because it dismantled feudal privileges and spread legal institutions (Britannica). Evidence A: "ended feudalism" supports this.'

materials: Copies of two short evidence slips per pair (teacher-prepared, 1 minute to photocopy) with one quotation each: (A) a line from the Encyclopaedia Britannica article summarising causes and dates, (B) a short summary sentence from Acemoglu et al. (2011) about long-term consequences, (C) a one-sentence claim from Opie (1997) about the guillotine as symbol, and (D) one bibliographic line from the further reading list (any author)
Timer or stopwatch (phone is fine)
Whiteboard and marker
Desk name cards or paper to label pair positions
student_instructions: You are in a pair and have been given two evidence slips (A and B). Read them silently during the 1-minute planning period.

Your goal is to argue for or against the motion: 'The French Revolution created the modern nation-state.' Use only classroom knowledge plus the two slips as the factual basis you must cite aloud at least once during your speech.

Follow the timing: 1 minute planning together; Pro opening 2 minutes (state main claims and cite one slip); Con opening 2 minutes (respond and cite one slip); 1 minute plan rebuttal; Pro rebuttal 2 minutes (answer Con and use any evidence); Con rebuttal 2 minutes; then listen for class vote.
When citing a slip, say its label and phrase (for example: 'Evidence A says…' or 'Acemoglu et al. show…'). If you use the Britannica slip, explicitly name it as 'Britannica'.
After the vote, one member from the winning and one from the losing side will say which slip mattered most and whether it supports more than one interpretation.
success_criteria: Most pairs cite at least one of their slips aloud during their opening or rebuttal.

Pairs follow the timing (speeches roughly the assigned length) and give an argument that connects either the Revolution's end/start dates or a long-term impact (land redistribution, nationalism, export of institutions) to their stance.
Two pairs (one from each side) can state which slip influenced them and whether it allows competing interpretations.
teacher_instructions: 1. Arrange students in pairs. Give each pair two evidence slips: one labelled Evidence A and one labelled Evidence B. Tell students they will use those slips during a 12-minute debate with timings signalled by you.

2. Announce the motion: 'This House believes the French Revolution created the modern nation-state.' Assign half the pairs to Pro and half to Con; if an odd number, teacher joins one side. Display the conventional dates and events from the class text on the whiteboard (e.g. start: 1789 — Estates-General / Storming of the Bastille; end: 1799 — Napoleon's coup) so all can reference them.

3. Run the timed sequence: 1 minute quiet planning, 2 minutes Pro opening, 2 minutes Con opening, 1 minute rebuttal planning, 2 minutes Pro rebuttal, 2 minutes Con rebuttal, 2 minutes class vote and quick justification. While running, keep strict time and quietly circulate to read pairs' slips and note if they cite their evidence slip during speeches.

4. After the vote, ask two pairs (one Pro, one Con) to each state which piece of evidence from their slips most influenced their argument and whether the evidence supports a unanimous interpretation or multiple readings; record one sentence from each on the whiteboard.

5. Close by reminding students of the conventional start/end events and dates on the whiteboard and asking students to write one line on their desk paper: 'One way the Revolution had a long-term impact is...' using evidence from their slip.
activities.title: Timed Debate: Did the French Revolution Create a Lasting Modern Nation-State?

items.answer: Start: The Storming of the Bastille on 14 July 1789. End: Napoleon Bonaparte's coup of 18 Brumaire, which took place on 9 November 1799 (the conventional end of the Revolution).

rubric.criteria: Accuracy in recalling the conventional start and end events and their exact dates.

levels.descriptor: Clearly names the Storming of the Bastille and gives the exact date 14 July 1789, and clearly names Napoleon's coup of 18 Brumaire and gives the exact date 9 November 1799.
levels.label: Full credit

levels.descriptor: Either (a) correctly gives one event with its correct date (e.g. Bastille and 14 July 1789 OR 18 Brumaire/coup and 9 November 1799) OR (b) names both events but gives an incorrect or missing date for one or both.
levels.label: Partial credit

levels.descriptor: Fails to identify either conventional event and date correctly (answers are incorrect, unrelated, or left blank).
levels.label: No credit

items.stem: According to the conventional dates given in the text, state the event and exact date commonly used to mark the start of the French Revolution, and the event and exact date commonly used to mark its end. (6 marks)

items.answer: Social: Rising inequality and public anger at privileges of the nobility and clergy — for example, urban workers and peasants faced high food prices and resented tax exemptions for elites. Economic/financial: A chronic fiscal crisis — repeated deficits from costly wars and an inefficient tax system left the state near bankruptcy, requiring unpopular borrowing and attempted reforms. Political: Indecisive royal policy and resistance to reform — ministers’ fiscal reforms were blocked by privileged estates and royal vacillation, producing stalemate. Interaction: Economic hardship increased popular grievances (social), while the crown’s inability to implement fair taxation (political) prevented resolution of the fiscal crisis, so anger at privilege and failed reform combined to radicalise opinion and precipitate revolution. (All points supported by chapter examples: food price rises, state deficits, blocked reform attempts and protests.)

rubric.criteria: Explains one social, one economic/financial and one political factor and shows briefly how they interacted to produce revolutionary crisis, using chapter evidence.

levels.descriptor: Identifies a clear social factor, a clear economic/financial factor, and a clear political factor drawn from the chapter (each named or quoted). Explains succinctly how these three interacted to create crisis (links economic hardship to social grievance and political failure to resolve it) and includes at least one chapter example or detail.
levels.label: 3 marks

levels.descriptor: Identifies two of the three required factors clearly and the third partially (e.g., named but not exemplified). Gives a reasonable explanation of interaction between factors but with limited evidence from the chapter (one example or a general reference).
levels.label: 2 marks

levels.descriptor: Names at least one relevant factor from the chapter (social, economic/financial or political) with minimal or no explanation of interaction and little or no chapter evidence; answer shows understanding but is fragmentary.
levels.label: 1 mark

items.stem: Explain, using evidence from the chapter, how social, economic/financial and political factors combined to create the crisis that led to the Revolution. In your answer give one example of each type of factor and explain briefly how they interacted to produce revolutionary pressure. (3 marks)

items.answer: They verified and registered their deputies, broke away from the Estates-General to sit separately as the National Assembly, and took the Tennis Court Oath promising not to disperse until a constitution was written — these are recorded, sequential actions the Third Estate took during the move from the Estates-General to the National Constituent Assembly.

options.label: A
options.rationale: Correct — each action is documented: Third Estate deputies checked and verified their membership rolls, declared themselves the National Assembly when they broke from the traditional order structure, and after being locked out they took the Tennis Court Oath to stay assembled until a constitution was agreed.
options.text: They verified and registered their deputies, broke away from the Estates-General to sit separately as the National Assembly, and took the Tennis Court Oath promising not to disperse until a constitution was written.

options.label: B
options.rationale: This option mixes later revolutionary outcomes and myths: the Third Estate did not immediately proclaim a republic or universally seize arms at that moment, nor did they unilaterally abolish feudal dues before constitutional work; those were later, sometimes separate, developments.
options.text: They immediately declared a republic, seized arms in Paris, and abolished feudal dues without waiting for any written constitution or assembly procedures.

options.label: C
options.rationale: This describes the opposite of what happened. The Third Estate refused to vote by order (they wanted head-count voting), did not simply accept an adjournment, and did not disband — instead they asserted a new assembly.
options.text: They joined the clergy and nobility in voting by order, accepted the king's demand to adjourn, and disbanded once the royal session ended.

options.label: D
options.rationale: This option contains chronological errors and false actions: the Declaration was not produced in May (it was adopted in August 1789), they did not invite foreign armies, and the monarchy was not abolished at the Estates-General opening.
options.text: They produced the Declaration of the Rights of Man and of the Citizen in May, invited foreign armies to enforce reforms, and abolished the monarchy on the day of the Estates-General opening.

items.stem: Between the calling of the Estates-General in May 1789 and the formation of the National Constituent Assembly, which list correctly identifies at least three concrete actions the Third Estate actually took during that sequence of events?

items.answer: Although the Bastille contained only a small number of prisoners when it was taken on 14 July 1789, the chapter shows that its fall became a powerful symbol of the Ancien Régime for several linked reasons. First, contemporary newspapers and pamphlets amplified the event: reporters and revolutionary writers spread vivid accounts and rumours that exaggerated the Bastille’s role as a site of political repression, so the public came to see its capture as the overthrow of despotism rather than merely the seizure of a small prison. Second, the revolutionary press and print culture deliberately redefined meanings and promoted new symbols to replace old-regime imagery; descriptions of the Bastille’s fall were integrated into a wider symbolic programme (alongside the tricolour and the liberty cap) that turned concrete events into shared political mythology. Third, pamphleteers and illustrators framed the Bastille as a physical embodiment of monarchical and clerical tyranny, giving the crowd’s action clear moral and political significance beyond any immediate practical result. Together, sensational reporting, deliberate symbolic construction, and the circulation of images and stories explain why the Bastille’s fall became a lasting emblem of the Ancien Régime despite the fortress’s small real role as a prison.

rubric.criteria: Explanation of why the Bastille’s fall became a potent symbol, citing media and symbolic construction from the chapter.

levels.descriptor: Explains clearly and specifically that the Bastille held few prisoners but became a potent symbol because newspapers and pamphlets amplified and sensationalised the event, popular rumours exaggerated its role, and revolutionary actors deliberately created and promoted new symbols (e.g. linking the Bastille with the tricolour and liberty cap). Uses the chapter’s points about print culture and symbolic redefinition to connect media amplification with the transformation of a local action into national political mythology.
levels.label: Excellent (6 marks)

levels.descriptor: States that the Bastille held few prisoners and that publicity made it symbolic. Mentions newspapers/pamphlets or the deliberate creation of symbols, but explanation is incomplete or fails to link media amplification to the deliberate symbolic programme described in the chapter, or gives only general statements without specific reference to how print culture created the myth.
levels.label: Partial (3 marks)

levels.descriptor: Fails to recognise that the Bastille held few prisoners or offers only factual errors (for example, claiming it held many political prisoners) and gives no coherent explanation of the role of newspapers, pamphlets, or symbolic construction from the chapter.
levels.label: Insufficient (0 marks)

items.stem: Using the chapter's description, explain why the Storming of the Bastille on 14 July 1789 became a potent symbol of the Ancien Régime even though the fortress held very few prisoners. In your answer, refer to the role of newspapers, pamphlets and the deliberate creation of revolutionary symbols.

items.answer: The August Decrees legally abolished feudalism by cancelling feudal dues and ended the obligation to pay church tithes; they also established legal equality (ending the seigneurial privileges). A practical difficulty in implementing these measures was local resistance and confusion over enforcement and compensation—landowners and clergy disputed what exactly was cancelled and how clergy were to be compensated (leading to reliance on assignats), making on-the-ground application uneven and contentious.

items.answer: Between September 1793 and July 1794 the Revolutionary government used a set of emergency measures to suppress perceived internal enemies. Key measures included the Law of Suspects (September 1793), which broadened grounds for arrest and led to mass imprisonment (around 300,000 people are estimated to have been arrested under Terror policies). Revolutionary tribunals carried out summary trials and executions: tribunal records indicate roughly 16,500–17,000 judicial executions in 1793–1794 (with notable spikes after the Law of 22 Prairial, passed on 10 June 1794, which simplified procedures and increased convictions). Extra-judicial repression also occurred: the Nantes drownings (often dated to 1793–1794) are estimated at around 1,800–2,000 victims, and there were many deaths in prisons and in the Vendée rising; when combined with executions the wider death toll of the Terror is commonly estimated at about 30,000–40,000. The period also included high-profile political purges used as examples: the Hébertists were executed in March 1794, Danton and his allies were executed on 5 April 1794, and Robespierre himself fell and was executed on 28 July 1794, which ended the Terror. In short, emergency legislation (Law of Suspects, Revolutionary tribunals, and the Law of 22 Prairial) produced mass arrests (c. 300,000), thousands of judicial executions (c. 16,500–17,000) and several thousand extra-judicial deaths (e.g. Nantes c. 1,800–2,000), contributing to a total death toll often placed in the tens of thousands by historians.

items.answer: Metropolitan debates about rights — between revolutionary reformers (including the Society of the Friends of the Blacks and some Jacobins) and pro-colonial, slaveholding interests — directly shaped events in the Caribbean by polarising opinion, provoking colonial resistance, and creating practical policy dilemmas for Paris. In Saint-Domingue the 1791 enslaved uprising (August 1791) erupted into a large-scale revolt that intersected with metropolitan disputes over whether rights should extend to free people of colour or to enslaved people. Colonial planters formed pro-slavery lobby groups and militias to defend their privileges; metropolitan abolitionists and some legislators argued for extending civil rights, while others in Paris sought to avoid wrecking the colonial economy. In response, the revolutionary government attempted a mix of concessions, coercion and administrative intervention rather than immediate universal emancipation. Key policy responses 1791–1793 included: (1) legislative and administrative debate and limited concessions in Paris on the status of free people of colour (metropolitan bodies debated and in practice some decrees and votes in 1791–1792 addressed their civil rights), which intensified planter hostility; (2) dispatch of republican commissioners to the colony (notably Sonthonax and Polverel in 1792) with instructions to preserve the colony for the Republic — they combined military measures with political measures, using offers of freedom to enslaved people who supported republican forces and issuing local emancipation measures in 1793 in areas under their control; and (3) increasingly radical national rhetoric and policy from Paris that opened the way for commissioners to take emancipationist steps. These responses show a contested process: metropolitan debates produced inconsistent and sometimes contradictory policies, colonial resistance shaped how measures were implemented, and commissioners on the ground made pragmatic, sometimes unilateral choices (including conditional or local emancipation) before the Convention’s formal abolition of slavery in 1794. Historians differ on emphasis — some stress metropolitan ideology as the driver, others the agency of colonial actors and commissioners — but the evidence supports a reciprocal influence where metropolitan debates framed possibilities and colonial crises pushed policy toward emancipationist measures by 1793.

items.answer: On 22 September 1792 the Convention formally abolished the monarchy and proclaimed the French First Republic, transferring sovereignty from a hereditary king to the nation and its elected representatives. Politically this marked a decisive break with the ancien régime: it removed the legal basis for royal authority, justified later actions such as the trial and execution of Louis XVI, and opened the way for new republican institutions and a politics based on popular sovereignty. The decision to start dating events from Year One (1792) was a symbolic and practical attempt to show that history itself had been reset; it legitimised revolutionary changes by framing them as the beginning of a new era and helped to de-Christianise public life by replacing the old calendar tied to the church. Historians offer competing interpretations: some view the proclamation and new dating as the culmination of revolutionary radicalisation and an assertion of ideological rupture, while others argue they were pragmatic responses to the collapse of monarchical authority and the need to unify the nation in wartime. In short, the proclamation transformed where political legitimacy was claimed to lie, and the Year One calendar reinforced that transformation by making the revolution’s break with the past visible in everyday civic life.

items.answer: Women were active and visible agents during the Revolution in several connected ways. As writers and agitators they produced political texts and petitions—for example Olympe de Gouges published the Declaration of the Rights of Woman (1791) and advocated for legal equality, while women like Madame Roland influenced opinion in political salons. Women also took part directly in street politics: the Women’s March on Versailles in October 1789 is a clear instance of collective action where market women and other protesters forced the royal family to move to Paris. From 1790 onwards women formed political clubs and societies (for example the Society of Revolutionary Republican Women) and organized meetings, petitions and demonstrations to press economic and political demands. Despite this activism, successive revolutionary authorities limited women’s formal political rights: the 1791 Constitution framed active citizenship in male terms and did not extend the vote or full political rights to women; the 1793 Constitution, while more radical in some social language, likewise did not grant women political rights. The response hardened in October 1793 when revolutionary authorities banned women’s clubs and suppressed many organized female political activities, partly because leaders (e.g., some Jacobins) viewed outspoken women as a threat to public order and to revolutionary definitions of citizenship. Historians debate these developments: some argue women’s activism demonstrates an expanded political culture that nonetheless excluded women legally, while others emphasize that the Revolution ultimately reasserted a gendered public sphere by denying formal rights and suppressing women’s associations.

Acemoglu et al. (2011) find that areas exposed to more intense revolutionary violence and radical reform during the French Revolution experienced persistently lower economic development and different political behaviour in the long run compared with less-exposed areas. Empirically, they show that communes closer to massacre sites and where revolutionary authorities implemented radical policies (for example, confiscation of properties and replacement of local elites) had lower levels of public goods provision, lower wealth indicators, and were less likely to vote for redistributionist parties even a century later. The authors support causality using geographic and historical variation (distance to epicentres of violence, timing of reforms), instrumental variables, and tests that rule out simple pre-revolutionary differences.

They propose two main mechanisms. First, a human-capital and elite-attrition mechanism: radical violence destroyed or drove out local elites and skilled administrators, disrupting investments in public goods and institutions; this loss of human capital reduced economic development. Second, a political-institutional mechanism: harsh revolutionary experiences changed political preferences and social trust, making populations more conservative about redistribution and less willing to support collective investment, which in turn affected long-term public goods provision and economic performance. The paper points to supporting evidence for both mechanisms (e.g. changes in occupational composition, slower recovery of public services, and altered voting patterns), and discusses how these interact rather than being mutually exclusive.

Refers to the types of evidence used (variation in exposure, distance to violence, instrumental strategies, voting and public-goods data) and connects evidence to mechanisms.

items.answer: An extensive bibliography helps the student see that historians approach the French Revolution from many angles rather than as a single agreed story. Three clear features that reveal this diversity are: (1) the variety of types of works listed (books, journal articles, edited collections, doctoral theses, and primary-source editions). This matters because books often present broad synthetic interpretations, articles advance focused arguments or new evidence, theses sometimes contain original archival work, and primary-source editions enable students to check evidence themselves—together these types show both synthesis and ongoing debate. (2) The range of topical focuses (political institutions and leaders, social and economic change, cultural and intellectual history, regional studies, gender and popular movements). This matters because it demonstrates competing causal explanations: for example, political-institutional accounts emphasize events and elites, social or economic studies stress class and material conditions, and cultural or gender studies highlight meanings, identities, and lived experience. Recognising these topics helps a student compare explanations and see how they complement or contradict one another. (3) The presence of different interpretive traditions and national or chronological perspectives (e.g., older Marxist or revolutionary-society interpretations, revisionist or cultural-history works, comparative studies placing France in a European or Atlantic context). This matters because historiographical traditions frame questions and evidence differently—Marxist accounts foreground class struggle and long-term structures, revisionists question teleological narratives and emphasise contingency, while comparative work situates the Revolution among broader processes. By noting these features, a student can map debates, evaluate evidence, and understand that interpretations depend on methods, sources, and questions the historian chooses.

Shows awareness of how these features affect questions, evidence, and causal claims about the Revolution.

items.answer: The Revolution grew out of an interlinked crisis across social, economic, financial and political spheres. Financially, long wartime spending (especially after the Seven Years' War) and the costs of supporting the American War left the royal treasury deeply in deficit; ministers’ attempts to raise revenue through broad-based taxation were blocked, producing repeated fiscal emergencies. Economically and socially, poor harvests, rising bread prices and stagnant wages increased popular hardship and peasant unrest, while the burden of indirect taxes and feudal dues fell disproportionately on the Third Estate. Politically, the monarchy faced paralysis: elite resistance (notably from the parlements and privileged nobility) blocked reforms proposed by ministers such as Turgot and Calonne, and Louis XVI’s vacillation meant reforms were introduced too late or half-heartedly. Resistance to reform therefore amplified the financial crisis (because needed tax changes failed) and deepened social grievances (because economic pain was not relieved). Although Enlightenment ideas and political pamphlets helped shape how people understood injustice, they were not the sole cause; rather, ideological currents interacted with concrete fiscal collapse, worsening living conditions, and a political system unable to resolve the crisis. These combined factors produced widespread mobilization and the collapse of royal authority that led to Revolution.

levels.descriptor: Clearly explains how financial collapse, economic hardship, social inequality and political paralysis interacted. Uses specific evidence from the chapter (e.g. wartime debts, failed ministerial reforms, poor harvests, tax burdens, parlements’ resistance, Louis XVI’s indecision) and links these causes to show how resistance to reform and indecisive royal policy intensified the crisis.

Mentions reform resistance or royal indecision but does not fully show how these amplified the crisis.

items.answer: After the Estates-General was summoned in May 1789 the Third Estate took a series of deliberate, public actions that transformed it from one estate among three into the basis of a new representative body. First, the Third Estate verified and published the credentials and lists of its deputies and insisted on voting by head rather than by order — a procedural stance that challenged the traditional privilege of the clergy and nobility and asserted the deputies' claim to equal representation. Second, when the usual meeting hall was closed or access was obstructed in June, the Third Estate moved to a nearby tennis court and took the Tennis Court Oath, swearing not to disperse until they had given France a constitution; this was a concerted public oath that committed them to constitutional change and signalled a political break with the old procedures. Third, the Third Estate declared itself the National Assembly and invited sympathetic members of the clergy and nobility to join, thereby claiming to represent the nation as a whole rather than a single estate. Together these actions — verifying deputies and demanding voting by head, taking the Tennis Court Oath, and declaring a National Assembly while reaching out to other orders — changed the legal and political status of the deputies and advanced the move from estate-based consultation toward a constituent body empowered to draft a constitution. These steps made the Third Estate the focal point of national sovereignty and laid the groundwork for later acts such as the Declaration of the Rights of Man and of the Citizen (published 26 August 1789) during the constitutional drafting process.

levels.descriptor: Clearly names at least three concrete actions (e.g. verifying deputies/insisting on voting by head; taking the Tennis Court Oath; declaring the National Assembly and inviting clergy/nobles) and explains, in sequence, how each action advanced the Third Estate from an estate delegation to a constituent national assembly; links actions to claims of national representation or constitutional commitment.

levels.descriptor: Names one or two correct actions or names three actions but gives only brief or unclear explanation of their sequence or significance; some accurate connection to change in status is made but lacks detail or precision.
levels.label: Partial credit

levels.descriptor: Fails to identify any correct concrete actions or gives descriptions that are inaccurate or irrelevant; no coherent explanation of how actions changed the Third Estate's status.

Assignats: A paper currency backed by confiscated church property used by the revolutionary government.
Assignats were meant to fix finances but led to rising prices and inflation before later monetary changes.
Reign of Terror: The period (approx. Sept 1793 to July 1794) when revolutionary governments used emergency laws, mass arrests, and executions against perceived enemies of the Revolution.
Important measures and events:
- Law of Suspects (authorised arrests of suspected opponents)
- Law of 22 Prairial (expanded procedures for conviction and execution)
- Guillotine: Execution device invented during the Revolution; became the principal symbol of the Terror
- Drownings at Nantes (mass executions by drowning)
- Executions of Hébertists and Danton (prominent political figures executed during the Terror)
- Execution of Robespierre (July 1794) — end of the main Terror period
diagrams_to_draw: A simple horizontal timeline from 1792 to 1794 marking: '22 Sept 1792: Republic proclaimed', 'Sept 1793: start of main Terror measures', 'July 1794: execution of Robespierre — Terror ends'.

checkpoint_questions.expected_answer: Law of Suspects — allowed wide arrest of those 'suspected' of opposing the Revolution; Law of 22 Prairial — sped up trials and reduced defendants' rights, increasing the rate of convictions and executions.

checkpoint_questions.question: Give two specific examples of the human costs or acts of repression the text mentions during the Terror.

anticipated_questions: Will we be graded on the ticket? (No — it's just for thinking.)
Can I change my view later? (Yes — we'll compare ideas to facts.)
What counts as an example? (Any short image, name, or event you associate.)

teacher_script.heading: Collect entry tickets and quick share
teacher_script.speaker_notes: Ask students to hand in or hold up their one-sentence tickets. Read aloud 3 different answers you collected that represent different views: one that calls the Terror necessary, one that calls it a mistake, and one that gives a different idea. Say: "Keep those reactions in mind — today we'll use facts to test these quick impressions." Tell students: "If your answer mentioned the guillotine, assignats, or a name (Robespierre, Danton, Hébert), listen for where that appears in the facts I will give."

anticipated_questions: Did the new calendar replace months and weekdays? (Yes — the Convention introduced a new calendar; we are only noting that Year One began in 1792.)
Were assignats real money? (Yes — they were paper currency backed by church property.)

If assignats were backed by land, why did they cause inflation? (Students often ask this; say: we'll explore that in the discussion — the confiscated assets did not stop prices rising when too many assignats circulated.)
teacher_script.board_action: Write the three full sentences exactly as read. Underline the words: "Year One (1792)", "Assignats", and "inflation".
teacher_script.heading: Introduce key facts: Republic, calendar, assignats
teacher_script.speaker_notes: Say: "I will list the main facts you must remember. Listen and copy exactly what I put on the board." Read each fact slowly and point to the board lines as you write them. Say the date aloud when you write it. Use these sentences to read: 1) "22 September 1792: The Convention declared the French First Republic and started a new calendar, beginning Year One (1792)." 2) "Assignats: A paper currency backed by confiscated church property used by the revolutionary government." 3) "Assignats were meant to fix finances but led to rising prices and inflation before later monetary changes." Pause after each sentence to let students copy. When you write "inflation," give a quick concrete example: "Bread prices rising so wages buy less."

anticipated_questions: What exactly did the Law of Suspects do? (It authorised arrests of people suspected of opposing the Revolution; details will be discussed in sources later.)
Who were the Hébertists and Danton? (Short answer: political group/members; Danton was a leading revolutionary; both were executed during the Terror.)
Was Robespierre only a victim? (Students may ask; say: he was a leader associated with the Terror and was executed in July 1794.)
teacher_script.board_action: Write the sentence for "Reign of Terror" as given in the definitions. Below it list: "Law of Suspects", "Law of 22 Prairial", "Guillotine (symbol of the Terror)", "Drownings at Nantes", "Executions of Hébertists and Danton", "Execution of Robespierre".
teacher_script.heading: Describe the Reign of Terror facts and figures
teacher_script.speaker_notes: Read this paragraph aloud while pointing to the board: "Reign of Terror (approx. Sept 1793 to July 1794): revolutionary governments used emergency laws, mass arrests and executions against perceived enemies. Important measures included the Law of Suspects and the Law of 22 Prairial. Violence included public executions by guillotine, drownings at Nantes, the execution of prominent Hébertists and Danton, and eventually the execution of Robespierre." After reading, ask: "Which of those items names a law, which names people, which names methods of execution?" Call on volunteers and prompt them to point at the words on the board. Then say: "These are the measures and human costs you must be able to summarise."

anticipated_questions: Can we use outside facts? (Use only the facts on the board for this task.)

teacher_script.board_action: Add the instruction: "Group task: 2 supporting facts + 1 challenging fact. Choose a speaker." Leave previous facts visible.
teacher_script.heading: Group discussion: competing interpretations with evidence
teacher_script.speaker_notes: Put students in groups of 3. Give this instruction aloud and post it on the board: "Each group: pick one view from the opening tickets (necessary, mistake, or other). Spend 5 minutes finding two facts on the board that best support that view and one fact that challenges it. Appoint one speaker for your group." Walk around and listen. After 5 minutes call two groups to report: ask the speaker to name their chosen view, the two supporting facts, and the one challenging fact. If a group chooses "assignats solved the crisis," ask them to find the board line that says assignats caused inflation.

anticipated_questions: Can we use notes? (Yes — but only from what you've copied from the board.)
What if we run out of time? (Keep arguments short — one clear point with one board fact.)
Can the witness read more than one fact? (Stick to one clear fact to keep timing fair.)
teacher_script.board_action: Write the role list and timing: "Prosecutor 40s, Defender 40s, Witness reads board fact 40s". Keep facts visible.
teacher_script.heading: Role-play courtroom: who is responsible?
teacher_script.speaker_notes: Explain: "We will do a quick 5-minute courtroom. I will be the judge who times speakers. You need three roles: prosecutor (blames revolutionary government), defender (blames external threats/war), and witness (reads a fact from the board). Groups of 4 will send one representative to a single court in front of the class. Each role gets 40 seconds. Prosecutor must cite at least one law or method from the board. Defender must cite at least one cause (use the Republic claim or external threat). Witness reads a fact exactly from the board." Run two short courts with volunteers. Prompt speakers: "Cite the board line you're using." After both courts, ask the class: "Which side used the Law of Suspects or assignats as evidence?"

anticipated_questions: Do we have to include exact dates? (Include the period Sept 1793 to July 1794 if you can.)
What counts as a number? (A date or the name of a law or person from the board.)
Will we keep these notes? (Yes — copy the board before you leave.)
teacher_script.board_action: Add the prompt for the one-sentence check and underline the words: "Sept 1793 to July 1794" and "use at least one name or number."
teacher_script.heading: Check understanding and consolidate
teacher_script.speaker_notes: Say: "Quick check: write one sentence that answers: Between Sept 1793 and July 1794, what measures were used and what were the human costs? End by summarising: "The Convention proclaimed the Republic on 22 Sept 1792. The Reign of Terror used emergency laws, mass arrests and executions (Sept 1793–July 1794). Assignats were paper money backed by church land but led to inflation."

Ideas — evidence: Declaration of the Rights of Man; Enlightenment authors cited in chapter
Practical problems — evidence: fiscal crisis, Assignats, food shortages, wartime mobilization (chapter's figures show troop increase)
Wartime mobilization → larger army; political reliance on army; faster use of military to resolve politics; leads to 18 Brumaire

diagrams_to_draw: Simple two-column table labelled 'Ideas' and 'Practical problems' with one evidence point under each

checkpoint_questions.expected_answer: Ideology view: Enlightenment ideas and radical political thought motivated revolutionary change. Pragmatic-crisis view: Immediate fiscal collapse, food shortages, and political conflicts forced practical responses that drove actions more than pure ideology.
checkpoint_questions.question: State, in one sentence, the two competing interpretations the chapter gives for what drove the Revolution: (a) the ideology view and (b) the pragmatic-crisis view.

checkpoint_questions.expected_answer: The chapter cites figures showing the army grew from small professional forces to a mass conscripted force (chapter figures): dramatically increased troop numbers and budgets, and reliance on levée en masse that made generals politically important.
checkpoint_questions.question: Give one piece of evidence the chapter uses to support the idea that wartime mobilization changed the French army's scale or political power between 1792 and 1795.

checkpoint_questions.expected_answer: Institutional weakness: a weak executive of five directors with a bicameral legislature that produced slow decision-making. Political consequence: reliance on the army and corruption increased, producing chronic violence and the conditions for 18 Brumaire.
checkpoint_questions.question: Using the Directory as described in the chapter, name one institutional weakness and one political consequence of that weakness.

entry_ticket.expected_response: One sentence choosing either 'Enlightenment ideas' or 'practical problems', plus one brief reason (e.g. 'Enlightenment ideas because the Declaration inspired action' or 'practical problems because money and war forced decisions').
entry_ticket.prompt: Write one short sentence answering: Which caused more of the French Revolution's actions between 1789–1799 — Enlightenment ideas (political theory) or immediate practical problems (money, food, war)? Then write one reason for your choice. Be honest — there are no right or wrong grades.

exit_ticket.prompt: In one short paragraph, compare the chapter's two interpretations about whether Enlightenment ideology or pragmatic crises best explain revolutionary actions. Give one specific piece of evidence from the chapter that the authors use for each interpretation. Then, in two sentences, describe how wartime mobilization changed the French military and political dynamics between 1792 and 1795, citing at least one figure or quantitative point the chapter gives.
exit_ticket.success_indicator: One paragraph that: (1) names both interpretations and gives one distinct chapter-cited piece of evidence for each; (2) then two sentences describing how mobilization expanded the army and shifted politics, and includes at least one chapter figure or quantitative point (for example troop numbers, percentage growth, or budget increase) to support the claim.

homework.submission_format: One uploaded document (paragraph + link or file for the 90-second summary) and a typed list of your question.
tasks: Write a 250-word paragraph that evaluates which interpretation (ideology or pragmatic crisis) you find more convincing for the period 1789–1795. Use two specific pieces of evidence from the chapter — one supporting each interpretation — and explain which evidence you trust more and why.
Create a 90-second audio or written summary that explains how wartime mobilization changed the size of the French army and its political role. Include the chapter figure(s) you will quote in class.
Bring one question about the Directory's reliance on the army or about the ideology debate to the next lesson to discuss in small groups.

mentor_moment.takeaway: Disagreement is normal in history; use the chapter's evidence to support your view, and listen for good evidence in opposing arguments.

Can I change my answer later? (Yes — the class will discuss different views.)
teacher_script.board_action: Write two column headers: 'Ideas' and 'Practical problems'. Under each, leave space for students to add one example later.
teacher_script.heading: Collect entry tickets and show common answers
teacher_script.speaker_notes: Collect the quick sentences. While you hand them in, read three aloud (pick one that says 'ideas', one that says 'problems', and one in between). Say: 'Thanks. You can keep thinking about that question. For today we will compare those two views using the chapter's evidence.'

anticipated_questions: Was the Directory the same as a king? (No — it was an executive collective of five directors, not a monarch.)
Why five directors? (The chapter explains this was designed to avoid a single ruler after the Terror.)
teacher_script.board_action: Under the earlier headings add one short line under the board's middle area: 'Directory: 5 directors; bicameral legislature; weak executive; relied on the army; corruption'.
teacher_script.heading: Introduce the Directory and the historical problem
teacher_script.speaker_notes: Hold up the chapter and point to the heading 'Directory (1795–1799)'. Say: 'The Directory governed after the Reign of Terror. It had a weak executive—five directors—and a two-house legislature. It faced political unrest, economic weakness, and relied on the army. Today we will see how war and money problems shaped the Directory and how historians disagree about ideas vs. problems.' Read aloud this one-sentence summary from the chapter: 'The Directory was weak, corrupt, and dependent on the army.' Then ask: 'What would a government dependent on the army look like? Give one quick idea.' Call on two students to answer.

anticipated_questions: Is the chapter saying one view is right? (No — it presents both as competing interpretations.)
Which view do most historians accept? (Historians disagree; the chapter says both matter.)
What is an Assignat again? (A paper currency backed by confiscated church property — taught earlier.)
teacher_script.board_action: Under 'Ideas' write one evidence: 'Declaration of the Rights of Man; Enlightenment authors cited.' Under 'Practical problems' write one evidence: 'Fiscal crisis, Assignats, food shortages, war mobilization.'
teacher_script.heading: Compare two interpretations about ideology vs pragmatism
teacher_script.speaker_notes: Say: 'Now we compare two interpretations the chapter gives.' Read or paraphrase the two short positions: 1) 'Radical Enlightenment view: Enlightenment ideas — rights and popular sovereignty — motivated many revolutionary actions.' 2) 'Pragmatic response view: Immediate fiscal crisis, food shortages, and war forced many decisions more than pure theory.' For each view ask the class to give one piece of evidence the chapter uses. Pause and point at the page: 'For the ideas view the chapter cites Enlightenment authors and the Declaration. For the pragmatic view the chapter cites tax crisis, Assignats, and mobilization for war.' Ask students to turn to a partner and agree on one sentence evidence for each view. After 90 seconds, ask two pairs to share.

anticipated_questions: Can we use both sides' evidence? (You must pick a side, but you can explain why the other side might also have a point.)
What figures on army size? (The chapter's figures showing troop increases and conscription — point to the figures in the chapter.)
Can one person be the speaker? (Yes — choose one presenter for your group.)
teacher_script.board_action: Write on the board: 'Debate task: 2 points — evidence + explanation. Use chapter figures on army size and conscription.'
teacher_script.heading: Guided preparation for a short debate in groups
teacher_script.speaker_notes: Explain the quick task: 'In your groups of four, pick one side: Ideas or Practical problems. Use the chapter's evidence to prepare two short points: one piece of evidence and one explanation of why it shows your side matters. I will give you a minute to choose and eight minutes to prepare.' Hand out or point to two figures in the chapter that show army size and conscription change; say: 'Use those figures to support the 'practical problems' side if you can.' Walk the room, listening, and prompt one group with: 'Which figure from the chapter backs your claim? Read the caption aloud.'

anticipated_questions: What if our group runs out of time? (Say the key point quickly — evidence then why it matters.)
Do we need to mention the Directory now? (Yes — tie your point to how these causes affected the Directory.)
teacher_script.board_action: Create a quick tally column: 'Changed mind' and mark tallies as students raise hands.
teacher_script.heading: Structured mini-debate and small-group reflection
teacher_script.speaker_notes: Call three groups to present: one group arguing 'Ideas', one arguing 'Practical problems', and one that split the difference. Each group has one minute to speak. After each presentation, ask the class one quick question: 'What single piece of evidence did they use?' After the three, ask: 'Who changed their mind from the entry ticket? Raise your hand if you did.'

anticipated_questions: Do we need exact numbers for troop growth? (For now cite the chapter's figures — later you will copy exact numbers for homework.)
Why did directors fear the army? (Because the chapter shows the Directory depended on military force to govern and to put down unrest.)
What is 18 Brumaire? (A later coup that overthrew the Directory — taught in a later period.)
teacher_script.board_action: Underneath the Directory summary add: 'Wartime mobilization → larger army; political reliance on army; quicker coups (e.g. 18 Brumaire).' Add a short line: 'Check: cite the chapter's figures on troop growth.'
teacher_script.heading: Role play to show how wartime mobilization changed politics, then check
teacher_script.speaker_notes: Set up role play: 'Five volunteers will be 'Directors'. Two will be 'army commanders'. The rest decide quickly: will you support calling more troops or refusing? Directors must decide by a show of hands. Use the chapter figures (I will point at them) showing troop growth to imagine pressure on directors. Run the role play for three minutes. Then ask: 'How did reliance on the army shape the directors' choices?' End with a two-minute consolidation: ask one student to state one sentence describing how wartime mobilization changed military scale and one sentence about how that affected politics — and to cite 'the chapter's figures' or the chapter as the source.

anticipated_questions: What if we can't find the exact figures tonight? (Bring an approximate number and the page number; we will check together.)
Is this graded? (This is for learning and for tomorrow's discussion.)
teacher_script.board_action: Write as the exit prompt: 'Exit: ideology contested. Evidence (ideas) — Declaration; (problems) — fiscal crisis, Assignats, war mobilization. Bring one exact figure on troop numbers for homework.'
teacher_script.heading: Final check and consolidation
teacher_script.speaker_notes: Ask: 'In one sentence: does the chapter present ideology as the sole cause or a contested cause? And give one piece of evidence for both sides.' Call on two students. Then say: 'Tonight: read the chapter figures on conscription and troop numbers and bring one exact figure each for tomorrow.' Collect any last questions and dismiss.

Thermidorian reaction: revenge killings (south); executions of Commune leaders; repeal of Law of 22 Prairial; closure of Jacobin Club; negotiated peace treaties
Colonial tensions: abolitionist vs pro-slavery groups; uprisings in Saint-Domingue; commissioners tried measures; Convention abolished slavery in 1794 — enforcement and restrictions varied

Economic changes: abolition of tithes; nationalisation of church lands; assignats issued (backed by confiscated lands) → severe inflation and disruption; end of guilds and tax farming; later monetary stabilisation with Franc germinal (1803)
Definitions: La Marseillaise (1792; adopted 1795); Guillotine (symbol of the Terror); Liberty cap (Phrygian cap); Cockade (tricolore)
Practical difficulty with August Decrees: local enforcement and unclear ownership made collection of dues/tithes hard

Simple flow arrow: Church lands confiscated → Assignats issued → Assignats circulate → Inflation rises

checkpoint_questions.expected_answer: Because the Bastille had long stood as a visible emblem of royal authority and arbitrary power; popular rumours exaggerated its role as a prison, and the dramatic act of taking it made it a clear, memorable image that represented broader grievances. The chapter notes it held about seven prisoners, so its importance was symbolic rather than because of mass imprisonment.
checkpoint_questions.question: Using the chapter's description, why did the Storming of the Bastille become such a powerful symbol of the Ancien Régime even though the fortress held only a few prisoners?

checkpoint_questions.expected_answer: They abolished feudal dues and ended the collection of church tithes. A practical difficulty was enforcing these changes locally: peasants and landlords disputed what counted as dues, officials lacked clear records, and implementation varied by region, so old practices sometimes continued despite the new law.
checkpoint_questions.question: Name the immediate legal changes the August Decrees made about feudal dues and church tithes, and give one practical difficulty the chapter reports in putting those changes into practice.

checkpoint_questions.expected_answer: The government nationalised church lands and used them to back assignats as a way to pay debts. But assigning paper money against land did not stop rising prices; assignats multiplied in circulation, lost value, and helped drive severe inflation and economic disruption before later monetary reform.
checkpoint_questions.question: Explain how confiscating church property and issuing assignats related to France's fiscal crisis and to inflation, according to the chapter.

entry_ticket.expected_response: A: Seven prisoners. B: It was more important as a symbol of the Ancien Régime than for the number of prisoners.
entry_ticket.prompt: Write one short sentence answering both parts: (A) How many prisoners were held in the Bastille when it was stormed? (B) Was the Bastille more important because of the number of prisoners or because of what it symbolised?

exit_ticket.prompt: In one clear paragraph, explain how debates in metropolitan France about 'rights' affected the situation in the colonies—especially Saint-Domingue—and summarize the main French policy responses between 1791 and 1793.
exit_ticket.success_indicator: Paragraph mentions metropolitan debates over rights reaching the colonies; notes slaveholders' resistance and the rise of abolitionist and pro-slavery groups; describes uprisings in Saint-Domingue and commissioners sent to the colony; and explains that policies from 1791–1793 stopped short of full metropolitan equality, producing contested, uneven responses that set the stage for later 1794 abolition.

tasks: Select the chapter passage about the Bastille and write a one-page (250–300 word) explanation of how symbolic meaning can be stronger than factual details. Use at least two quotations from the passage and explain them.

Write a single-page (250–300 word) analysis that links the nationalisation of church lands, the creation of assignats, and the rise in inflation. Cite one sentence from the chapter as evidence and explain how it supports your point.

mentor_moment.story: A teacher brought a faded tricolour to class and asked why students cared about it more than a list of laws. They said the flag made the Revolution feel real. The teacher used that to show how symbols shape memory and political action.
