teacher_script.heading: Collect entry tickets and surface the Bastille myth
teacher_script.speaker_notes: Ask students to hold up their paper. Read aloud three student sentences (one that says many prisoners, two that say few or symbolic). Say: “We will start by checking these answers against the chapter. Tell me: how many prisoners does the chapter report?” Pause for answers. If a student says 'many', show the correction: “The chapter reports only seven prisoners.” Then say: “Write down the short phrase I give you: 'Bastille = symbol more than prison.' We will return to why symbols can beat facts.”

anticipated_questions: What was the Law of 22 Prairial?
Who were the Commune leaders?
Do 'negotiated peace treaties' mean France stopped fighting?
teacher_script.board_action: Write heading: Thermidorian reaction. Bullet list with the five items: revenge killings (south), executions of Commune leaders, repeal of Law of 22 Prairial, closure of Jacobin Club, negotiated peace treaties.
teacher_script.heading: Introduce Thermidorian reaction and recent changes
teacher_script.speaker_notes: Say: “Now I will describe the political shifts after Robespierre. Listen for actions and for where they happened.” Read aloud a short list: "revenge killings in southern France; executions of Commune leaders; repeal of the Law of 22 Prairial; closure of the Jacobin Club; negotiated peace treaties." After reading, point at each item and ask: “Which of these sounds like reversing radical Terror policies? Which sounds like moving toward compromise?” Call on two volunteers to answer. Then say: “Keep these as examples of Thermidorian reaction: it was a political turn and a mix of revenge and negotiation.”

anticipated_questions: Did abolitionists win immediately?
If the Convention abolished slavery, why were there still restrictions?
What did the commissioners do exactly in Saint-Domingue?
teacher_script.board_action: Draw four labeled boxes: Abolitionists, Planters, Commissioners, Rebels. Under each box, write one short phrase the groups used in their role lines.
teacher_script.heading: Guided role play: metropolitan debates and the colonies (focus on Saint-Domingue)
teacher_script.speaker_notes: Explain the activity: “You will role-play four groups for four minutes each: (1) metropolitan abolitionists, (2) metropolitan pro-slavery planters, (3) commissioners in Saint-Domingue, (4) enslaved rebels in Saint-Domingue. I will give each group one sentence from the chapter to read and one action to propose.” Hand out short slips (read these aloud if necessary): Abolitionists: argue for universal rights; Planters: argue for property and order; Commissioners: report on uprisings and try negotiated measures; Rebels: demand freedom and resist limits. Tell each group to pick one short sentence to say to the class. After four minutes, each group speaks one line in order. After the role play, ask: “According to the chapter, what legal step did the Convention take in 1794?” (pause) Confirm: abolition of slavery in 1794, but enforcement and restrictions varied. End with: “Note how metropolitan debates changed practical policy in the colonies.”

anticipated_questions: Why did assignats cause inflation if they were backed by land?
What were the August Decrees exactly?
Did everyone accept confiscation of church lands?
teacher_script.board_action: Write heading: Economic policies & consequences. Bullets: abolition of tithes; nationalisation of church lands; assignats issued → inflation; end of guilds and tax farming; later Franc germinal (1803).
teacher_script.heading: Explain economic measures: church property, assignats, and inflation
teacher_script.speaker_notes: Say: “Listen while I connect three facts from the chapter: confiscation of church lands, use of those lands to back assignats, and the inflation that followed.” Point to the board items you will write. Read aloud a clear causal sequence: confiscate church land → issue assignats to raise revenue → assignats circulate as paper money → widespread inflation and economic disruption. Ask: “What practical problem did the chapter give for implementing the August Decrees on tithes and feudal dues?” Wait for answers; prompt with: “Think of local records, people resisting, or unclear land ownership.” Confirm the chapter mentions practical difficulties collecting or enforcing the new rules. Emphasize later stabilization: mention Franc germinal in 1803 as later monetary reform but do not explain beyond the name and date.

anticipated_questions: Do we need to memorise the year 1794 for slavery?
Can you repeat the one practical example of difficulty with August Decrees?
Will there be a document question about the Bastille?
teacher_script.board_action: Underline four objective labels already present on the board and add a two-item 'Copy before leaving' list: (1) Bastille = symbol not mass prison (7 prisoners), (2) Convention abolished slavery 1794 but enforcement varied.
teacher_script.heading: Check for understanding and consolidate the four objectives
teacher_script.speaker_notes: Say: “We will check the four objectives from the chapter. I will read each objective and you give a one-sentence answer aloud.” Read objective 1: Bastille symbol — call on a volunteer to answer. Read objective 2: August Decrees legal changes and one implementation difficulty — call a different volunteer. Read objective 3: relationship of church confiscation, assignats, and inflation — call another volunteer. diagnostic_questions.question: You have three short sources: (A) an extract from Montesquieu on rights, (B) a 1788 royal finance report showing huge deficits and bankruptcy risk, (C) a petition from Paris workers complaining about bread shortages and unemployment. Which of these best explains why the Revolution actually began in 1789? Explain your choice in one sentence.
diagnostic_questions.reveals: If the student picks A (Montesquieu) as the best explanation, it reveals they favor an ideology-only causal story and underweight concrete fiscal and social evidence.

diagnostic_questions.expected_wrong_answer: The pamphlet/ideas claim — I'd use Rousseau or other Enlightenment writings as my primary evidence.
diagnostic_questions.question: Historians disagree about causes. Which is a stronger claim supported by contemporary evidence for immediate causation in 1789: 'Enlightenment pamphlets changed minds and thus caused the uprising' or 'a fiscal crisis and shortages made rebellion likely immediately'? Give the one you think is stronger and one piece of primary evidence you would use.
diagnostic_questions.reveals: If the student chooses the pamphlet/ideas claim and cites only philosophical texts (not contemporaneous financial records, price data, or petitions), it reveals they prioritise ideological explanations over immediate material crises despite documentary evidence.

evidence.quote: The Revolution resulted from multiple long-term and short-term factors, culminating in a social, economic, financial and political crisis in the late 1780s.

The role of ideology in the Revolution is controversial with Jonathan Israel stating that the "radical Enlightenment" was the primary driving force of the Revolution. Cobban, however, argues "[t]he actions of the revolutionaries were most often prescribed by the need to find practical solutions to immediate problems"

learning_gaps.misconception: The French Revolution happened because Enlightenment ideas (like liberty and natural rights) spread and made people overthrow the old regime — ideas alone caused the Revolution.

remediation.action: Document jigsaw: give small groups one primary source type each (philosophical pamphlet/Declaration excerpt; royal finance report/estate accounts; price lists/food riot petitions; local noble resistance records). Each group identifies what causal claim their document supports and two specific phrases or figures that support it, then students reform into mixed groups to combine evidence and produce a ranked list of immediate causes for 1789 with quotations or data.
remediation.rationale: Working directly with the different kinds of contemporary evidence forces students to ground causal claims in the historical record instead of relying on generalisations about 'ideas'. Combining groups demonstrates that multiple, different types of evidence point to different causal roles (ideology, fiscal collapse, economic hardship, political stalemate), countering the single-cause inference.

remediation.action: Cause-and-effect timeline: students place dated items (e.g. bad harvests, rising bread prices, 1786-88 finance reports, Necker's recall, publication dates of key Enlightenment works, Estates-General convocation) on a classroom timeline and attach a one-sentence note saying whether each item is primarily ideological, material/fiscal, or political. Teacher then leads a class discussion comparing which items immediately preceded mass mobilisation in 1789.
remediation.rationale: A chronological map shows sequencing and contingency — students see that many material and fiscal shocks cluster just before 1789 while Enlightenment works circulated earlier and more diffusely. This highlights causation and context rather than treating ideas as a single, proximate cause.

remediation.action: Historiographical role-play: assign students brief positions drawn from actual scholarly interpretations (e.g. 'Radical Enlightenment emphasis', 'fiscal-crisis interpretation', 'social-conflict view') with a short list of two supporting primary sources each. Students present a two-minute argument citing their sources, then peers ask for specific documentary evidence that would refute their claim.
remediation.rationale: Framing competing interpretations as evidence-based arguments models how historians weigh and contest causes. Requiring students to cite and to defend against counter-evidence trains them to move from attractive single-cause stories to nuanced, evidence-linked explanations.

diagnostic_questions.expected_wrong_answer: Yes — once the Third Estate declared the National Assembly, the old government was finished and the Assembly took power right away.
diagnostic_questions.question: After the Third Estate declared itself the National Assembly in 1789, did that declaration immediately replace the king's authority and make the Assembly the functioning government of France? Explain briefly.
diagnostic_questions.reveals: If the student answers 'yes' (or says the king's government ended immediately), it shows they treat the declaration as an instantaneous legal transfer rather than a contested political claim needing recognition and time.

diagnostic_questions.expected_wrong_answer: It was just a boring formality to check names; it didn't affect politics, so the Third Estate's declaration was all that mattered.
diagnostic_questions.question: What was the point of the 'verification of deputies' and the roll-call and credentials process during the Estates-General — was it just a boring formality, or did it matter politically? Explain.
diagnostic_questions.reveals: If the student says it was only a formality, they miss how disputes over who could vote, who represented which estate, and who had legitimate seats shaped the Assembly's authority and the timing of its actions.

learning_gaps.misconception: The Third Estate simply walked out of the Estates-General and immediately declared itself the National Assembly, so the old regime collapsed at once and the National Assembly instantly became the new government.

remediation.action: Begin the lesson with a 6–8 minute primary-source timeline card-sort: give small groups dated extracts (e.g., invitation to convene Estates-General, deputies' verification lists, Sieyès excerpt, account of the Tennis Court Oath, a royal proclamation, a Paris newspaper report) and ask groups to arrange them in chronological order and attach a one-sentence note about whether each item expands, challenges, or recognises the Assembly's authority.
remediation.rationale: Handling contemporaneous documents forces students to see sequence and disagreement in the historical record rather than a single dramatized moment. Sorting texts that sometimes deny or contest the Assembly shows that recognition and legal standing were gradual and contested, addressing the compression error.

remediation.action: Pair two short contrasting contemporary accounts (e.g., an aristocratic letter critical of the deputies and a popular Paris pamphlet celebrating them). Ask students to list three claims each makes about who has the right to decide and then lead a whole-class comparison asking: whose account treats the Assembly as already legitimate and whose does not?
remediation.rationale: Comparing competing perspectives aligns with the pedagogical aim to present interpretations. It reveals that legitimacy was disputed and dependent on recognition by different groups, countering the idea of an immediate transfer of power.

remediation.action: Run a 10–12 minute role-play simulation: small groups represent the Third Estate deputies, the clergy, the nobility, the king's ministers, and Parisian public opinion. Give each group a short briefing and a decision prompt (e.g., whether to recognise the Assembly's vote). After choices, debrief which coalitions were needed for the Assembly to function and why verification and recognition mattered.
remediation.rationale: Acting out the positions makes students experience the political negotiations and shows that declarations only gain effect when other actors accept or are forced to accept them. This corrects the assumption that a declaration alone equals immediate governmental change.

diagnostic_questions.expected_wrong_answer: There were dozens or hundreds of prisoners, so the crowd stormed it to free a large number of political prisoners.
diagnostic_questions.question: On 14 July 1789 the crowd attacked the Bastille. How many prisoners were actually held there at that moment, and what does this number suggest about the main reason for the attack?
diagnostic_questions.reveals: If a student answers that many prisoners were held and the attack was mainly a rescue, they still believe the 'rescue of many prisoners' justification rather than a symbolic/strategic motive.

diagnostic_questions.expected_wrong_answer: D) testimonies from many freed prisoners.
diagnostic_questions.question: Which evidence best supports the idea that the Bastille's fall was primarily symbolic rather than a large-scale prison rescue: A) the number of prisoners recorded inside, B) contemporary pamphlets calling it a symbol of tyranny, C) the weapons and gunpowder found, or D) testimonies from many freed prisoners?
diagnostic_questions.reveals: If a student selects D (testimonies from many freed prisoners) they expect mass imprisonment and miss that archival records show very few prisoners and that publicity and symbolism drove the event.

evidence.quote: Although rumoured to hold many prisoners, the Bastille held only seven: four forgers, a lunatic, a failed assassin, and a deviant nobleman.

learning_gaps.misconception: They stormed the Bastille because it was full of political prisoners and the crowd was rescuing lots of people who were unjustly jailed.

remediation.action: Begin the lesson with a short source-comparison exercise: give students two primary-source extracts side by side — an inventory/registry or archival record listing the seven prisoners in the Bastille on 14 July 1789, and a revolutionary pamphlet or newspaper excerpt from the same week describing the Bastille as 'the prison of the nation' or claiming it held many political prisoners. Ask students to note differences in what each source emphasises and to answer: 'Which source shows how many people were actually there?'
remediation.rationale: Confronting the factual archival record next to the rhetorical/political pamphlet makes students see that factual evidence (prison registers) and propaganda (pamphlets) served different purposes. This addresses the root: students generalise from persuasive contemporary narratives; the exercise makes them weigh types of evidence rather than accepting dramatic accounts uncritically.

remediation.action: Run a short class activity mapping causes: after the source comparison, have students work in pairs to list concrete reasons for attacking the Bastille (e.g., arms and gunpowder, a symbolic target, fear of royal troops, few prisoners). Ask pairs to rank the reasons and justify their ranking using the two sources and one additional secondary summary sentence (from a textbook or historian) that states the Bastille held seven prisoners and had outsized symbolic value.
remediation.rationale: Making students generate and justify multiple causal explanations shifts them from a single-story rescue narrative to a more nuanced causal analysis rooted in evidence. Requiring citation of the archival and secondary evidence prevents reverting to the dramatic myth and trains them to privilege documentary support for causal claims.

remediation.action: Conclude with a brief reflective writing prompt: 'How and why did reports and rumours about the Bastille’s prisoners spread, and how did that shape the Revolution's memory of 14 July?' Ask students to cite the pamphlet and registry and to mention the role of newspapers and crowd rumours.
remediation.rationale: A focused reflection asks students to integrate the documentary facts with the larger media context that produced the myth. This cements understanding that the Bastille's importance was amplified by contemporary and later narratives, directly addressing the mistaken inference that many prisoners justified the storming.

diagnostic_questions.expected_wrong_answer: A — Assignats eliminated the fiscal crisis and prices stayed stable because they were backed by confiscated land.
diagnostic_questions.question: The National Assembly issued assignats backed by church lands to pay debts. Which of these best describes what happened over the next few years? A) Assignats eliminated the fiscal crisis and France enjoyed stable prices. B) Assignats reduced immediate debt pressures but were over-issued, leading to inflation and economic disruption until later monetary reform. C) Assignats had no effect and were ignored. Which do you choose and why?
diagnostic_questions.reveals: Choosing A (or defending it) shows the student believes the issuance of assignats was a permanent solution without serious negative consequences, ignoring evidence of inflation, price controls, and later reform.

diagnostic_questions.expected_wrong_answer: Prices would stay the same and people would keep accepting the notes because they're backed by land, so printed quantity doesn't matter.
diagnostic_questions.question: Imagine the government issues paper money supposedly backed by land, but then prints a lot more paper money than the value of that land. What would you expect to happen to prices and people's willingness to accept the notes?
diagnostic_questions.reveals: Answering that nothing would change or that backing alone prevents price rises shows failure to grasp the mechanism by which over-issuance erodes real value and public confidence, a central reason assignats contributed to inflation.

evidence.quote: the value of which was used to back a new paper currency known as assignats.
When this resulted in escalating inflation, the response was to impose price controls and persecute private speculators and traders, creating a black market.

learning_gaps.misconception: Once the Assembly issued assignats, France's fiscal crisis was solved and there were no serious long-term negative effects — the paper money fixed the debt problem and everything else followed smoothly.

remediation.action: Document comparison: give small groups a primary-source excerpt reporting grain prices, a merchants' complaint about assignats, and the Assembly's decree on issuing assignats, plus a simple timeline/graph of assignat quantity vs. measured price indices (sourced from the chapter's evidence). Ask groups to annotate where the documents agree or conflict and place the documents on the timeline.
remediation.rationale: Confronting students with contemporaneous evidence that links rising assignat issuance to price rises and social unrest forces them to reconcile the simple "backed so solved" story with messy historical data. This targets the root overgeneralisation by showing the sequence and contradiction in primary sources rather than repeating the correct answer.

remediation.action: Classroom simulation: give each student a fixed number of 'land cards' (representing backing) and tokens (currency). Start with parity (tokens equal land value). Run rounds where students trade basic goods (cards represent suppliers). After a few rounds, introduce extra tokens into circulation and let students record the price (in tokens) of a standard good each round. Debrief by comparing rounds and linking the game events to assignat over-issuance and loss of confidence.
remediation.rationale: A short experiential model makes the causal mechanism visible: when money supply exceeds backing and real output, prices rise and the currency is devalued. Experiencing changing prices and declining willingness to accept tokens addresses the misconception grounded in abstract 'backing' language.

remediation.action: Structured historiography jigsaw: assign short contrasting historian excerpts — one emphasising assignats as a necessary fiscal innovation, another emphasising their role in causing inflation and political instability — and have each student summarise their excerpt and then teach it to a peer. Finish with a class chart listing which parts of the problem each interpretation explains well and which it leaves out.
remediation.rationale: Presenting competing historical interpretations anchored in evidence shows students that the assignats question is debated and complex. It prevents a single-cause narrative and helps students evaluate claims against evidence, correcting the tendency to treat the issuance as an uncomplicated solution.

diagnostic_questions.expected_wrong_answer: Yes — the decree abolished them, so peasants would stop paying at once; the law made everyone equal immediately.
diagnostic_questions.question: The August Decrees declared the end of feudal dues and tithes in August 1789. Would you expect a peasant in a rural parish in late 1789 to immediately stop paying seigneurial dues and church tithes? Explain briefly.
diagnostic_questions.reveals: If the student answers that payments stopped immediately, they treat the decree as instant, effective law everywhere; that shows they hold the misconception that legal abolition = immediate social/economic change.

diagnostic_questions.expected_wrong_answer: (A) all landlords accepted the loss and were paid immediately, because the Assembly abolished feudalism so the matter was settled.
diagnostic_questions.question: Which happened after the August Decrees: (A) all landlords accepted loss of their rights and compensation was paid right away, (B) many local disputes continued and some seigneurial customs were converted into rents or contested in courts? Choose the best answer and say why.
diagnostic_questions.reveals: Choosing (A) shows the student believes abolition was uniformly implemented and settled quickly, ignoring evidence of messy, uneven local outcomes and later legal/political negotiation.

learning_gaps.misconception: When the Assembly issued the August Decrees they instantly and completely ended feudalism and made peasants equal everywhere — after that, former seigneurial privileges and tithes were gone and life changed overnight.

remediation.action: Present students with two short primary-source excerpts: (1) a clause from the August Decrees that declares the abolition of feudal rights, and (2) a contemporaneous local petition or a court record showing a peasant complaining about a landlord still demanding dues several months later. Ask pairs to list similarities and differences in what each source actually shows happened.
remediation.rationale: Confronting the national decree with a local document forces students to see the gap between declaration and practice; it anchors the abstract legal wording in concrete contested outcomes and provides evidence that implementation was uneven rather than instantaneous.

remediation.action: Run a brief role-play or simulation: half the class are 'National Assembly deputies' writing a decree phrased like the August Decrees; the other half are 'local officials, landlords, and peasants' who must respond in a short set of notes describing practical problems (collection, enforcement, compensation). Debrief by comparing intended law and practical responses.
remediation.rationale: This makes students articulate logistical, economic, and social barriers to immediate change and thus corrects the assumption that a law alone produced instant equality; it highlights the need for administration, negotiation, and subsequent legislation.

remediation.action: Show a short timeline (class-generated) that places the August Decrees alongside later actions (e.g., sale of church lands, actions on seigneurial dues, legal reforms) and ask students to annotate where evidence shows gradual change versus immediate change.
remediation.rationale: Creating a timeline with multiple sources emphasizes causation and sequence, demonstrating that 'abolition' was a process involving further laws, local negotiation, and time — addressing the root error of conflating declaration with instant reality.

diagnostic_questions.expected_wrong_answer: A. France was trying to make itself bigger under one leader.
diagnostic_questions.question: Between 1792 and 1797 how would you best describe why French armies were fighting across Europe: (A) France was trying to make itself bigger under one leader; (B) revolutionary France was defending itself and spreading revolutionary ideas while responding to coalitions of monarchies? Explain briefly.
diagnostic_questions.reveals: If the student chooses A, they treat the wars as primarily imperial and personalised to a leader, showing they conflate Revolutionary and Napoleonic motives.

diagnostic_questions.expected_wrong_answer: 2. A single coronation ceremony expanding borders.
diagnostic_questions.question: Which of these pieces of evidence most supports the idea that the early Revolutionary wars were ideological and mass-based rather than purely imperial? (Choose one) (1) Levee en masse calling up citizens for defence, (2) A single coronation ceremony expanding borders, (3) A monarch signing lands over to France.
diagnostic_questions.reveals: Picking (2) or (3) indicates the student expects top-down imperial actions rather than citizen mobilisation or ideological export; they overlook primary evidence like mass conscription and revolutionary proclamations.

learning_gaps.misconception: The French Revolutionary Wars were just France trying to conquer other countries so a single leader (like Napoleon) could make France bigger.

remediation.action: Show students two dated primary-source extracts side by side: (a) the 1793 levée en masse proclamation calling citizens to defend the Republic, and (b) Napoleon’s 1804 coronation description or an 1805 campaign order. Have students annotate each for stated purpose (defence, ideology, or conquest) and for who is called to act (citizens vs. army leaders).
remediation.rationale: Comparing contemporary documents forces students to ground explanations in evidence and to distinguish motives and actors across periods. The levée en masse reveals republican mass mobilisation and defensive rhetoric; the coronation text shows later personal rule. This corrects the over-generalisation by showing different sources of authority and aims.

remediation.action: Use a two-map exercise: first map the territorial changes and client republics created by French revolutionary armies up to 1797 (e.g., sister republics, Austrian losses), annotated with brief quotes from treaties like Campo Formio; second map Napoleonic conquests after 1804. Ask students to write one sentence summarising the dominant cause suggested by each map (ideology/coalition collapse vs. imperial ambition).
remediation.rationale: Maps plus treaty excerpts show that early gains often resulted from revolutionary reorganisation and treaties after coalition collapse, not solely from imperial planning. This ties concrete geography and diplomatic records to causal interpretation, preventing reliance on later Napoleonic imagery.

remediation.action: Run a short role-play or structured debate: half the class argues from 1793 revolutionary sources (representing French deputies, conscripts, and local Jacobins) that they are defending and spreading liberty; the other half presents the perspective of European monarchs forming coalitions, using diplomatic letters and proclamations. Debrief with the question: what motives do each side attribute to the other, and where is evidence?
remediation.rationale: Adopting contemporary perspectives helps students appreciate multiple causal forces—ideology, defence, and reaction by coalitions—so they stop reducing the wars to a single-person imperial drive. The requirement to cite contemporary statements anchors interpretations in context and sources.

diagnostic_questions.expected_wrong_answer: Yes — once they swore the Oath they had created a new constitution and effectively replaced the old regime.
diagnostic_questions.question: After the Tennis Court Oath, did France immediately have a written constitution and a new legal government because the deputies had sworn not to disperse?
diagnostic_questions.reveals: Whether the student thinks the Oath was itself a legal, binding constitutional act rather than an initiating political pledge in an ongoing process.

diagnostic_questions.expected_wrong_answer: Everyone recognised them immediately — the Oath made the deputies the new authorities across France.
diagnostic_questions.question: Who recognised the authority of the deputies after the Tennis Court Oath: only the deputies themselves, the king and his ministers immediately, or a wider set of institutions? (Choose the best short answer.)
diagnostic_questions.reveals: Whether the student understands the Oath's limited immediate legal effect and the continuing role of the king and other institutions in deciding political power.

learning_gaps.misconception: When the deputies swore the Tennis Court Oath they legally created a new constitution and replaced the old government right away — it was a single decisive act that made France a constitutional state.

remediation.action: Give students the short original text of the Tennis Court Oath and a one-paragraph contemporary report (e.g. a newspaper or an account from a deputy). Ask pairs to underline words that state goals versus words that claim legal force, then produce a two-sentence summary about what the Oath actually did at the time.
remediation.rationale: Working directly with primary sources highlights the Oath's language of intent and collective promise rather than legal imposition. Comparing it with an eyewitness account shows how contemporaries treated it — as a political claim that needed follow-up — correcting the 'single decisive act' inference.

remediation.action: Run a 12-minute simulated timeline activity: groups place 8 dated events on a timeline (Estates-General convened, Tennis Court Oath, king's response, formation of the National Constituent Assembly, abolition of feudal rights, publication of a constitution). After arranging them, students justify the sequence and identify which events were legal acts and which were political steps.
remediation.rationale: Constructing the sequence makes clear that the Oath sits among multiple steps and that legal change (a written constitution, laws) came later. Distinguishing 'political claim' versus 'legal enactment' addresses the root confusion born from compressive narratives.

remediation.action: Facilitate a short classroom comparison: present a modern example of an oath/election that creates immediate legal authority (e.g. a court verdict or a certified election result) and contrast it with the Tennis Court Oath using evidence (dates, who accepted authority). Ask students to write one paragraph explaining two differences.
remediation.rationale: Explicitly comparing the familiar immediate-legal-force model with the historical case helps students stop overgeneralising. Grounding each difference in documentary evidence (dates, who accepted or resisted the deputies) corrects the transfer of modern assumptions onto 1789 events.

periods.sequence_rationale: As the opening period, this lesson establishes how social, economic, financial and political crises and royal indecision produced a breaking point and explains the Estates‑General, the Third Estate's actions, the Tennis Court Oath, and the Storming of the Bastille; mastering these events prepares students to evaluate the August Decrees, the Declaration of the Rights of Man, and later crises such as the flight to Varennes.
periods.title: Origins: Causes, Estates‑General, Bastille

periods.sequence_rationale: Builds on the Estates‑General, Tennis Court Oath and Bastille events to show how the Assembly translated revolutionary pressure into legal change (August Decrees, Declaration) and how Louis XVI's flight led to the constitutional monarchy's collapse; prepares students to analyze the Republic's proclamation and the Reign of Terror as consequences of these breakdowns.
periods.title: From August Decrees to Constitutional Monarchy

periods.sequence_rationale: Builds on the fall of the monarchy, the August Decrees and the constitutional monarchy phase by explaining how the Convention declared the First Republic and moved to emergency governance. This period prepares students to evaluate the Directory's political problems and the Revolution's lasting effects in the following lesson.
periods.title: Republic Proclaimed and the Reign of Terror

periods.sequence_rationale: This period builds on the Republic Proclaimed and the Reign of Terror material (including Assignats and Terror repression) by showing how war, economic strain and political violence shaped the weak Directory. It prepares students to assess the Thermidorian reaction, colonial slavery debates, media and womens roles, and the Directorys collapse into 18 Brumaire.
periods.title: Directory, Ideology Debate, and Wars

periods.sequence_rationale: This period builds on the Directory period's discussion of political instability, contested ideology, and wartime pressures by tracing how those debates shaped colonial policy, economic measures, and symbolic politics; it prepares students to evaluate the Revolution's long-term consequences and historiography in the following readings on impact and scholarly interpretations.
periods.title: Revolutionary Aftershocks: Colonies, Economy, Symbols

periods.sequence_rationale: This period builds on the preceding study of Thermidorian reaction, colonial slavery, revolutionary symbols, women's roles, and economic policy by moving from immediate outcomes to long‑term consequences and how historians explain them; as the closing lesson it synthesises those threads and points students to the cited sources (Britannica, Opie, Acemoglu et al.) and the extensive bibliography for independent follow‑up.
periods.title: Long‑Term Impacts and Historiography
